strings.hub.orders.title: Religious Orders
strings.hub.orders.subtitle: The orders & congregations of the Church
strings.hub.orders.intro: From cloistered monks to sisters in the world's slums, the Church's religious orders each live the Gospel through a particular gift — a charism. Here are the great families of consecrated life and what sets each apart.
strings.sec.orders.monastic.title: Monastic Orders
strings.sec.orders.monastic.summary: The great houses of prayer and work, from St Benedict onward.
strings.art.orders.monastic.title: Monastic Orders
strings.art.orders.monastic.lead: The great houses of prayer and work, from St Benedict onward.
strings.ord.benedictines.name: Benedictines
strings.ord.benedictines.desc: Founded by St Benedict of Nursia around 529 at Monte Cassino, the oldest religious order in the West. They live under his Rule with its motto “ora et labora” — prayer and work — in self-governing monasteries.
strings.ord.cistercians.name: Cistercians
strings.ord.cistercians.desc: A reform of Benedictine monasticism begun at Cîteaux in 1098, seeking a stricter, simpler return to the Rule. St Bernard of Clairvaux made them one of the great forces of medieval Europe.
strings.ord.trappists.name: Trappists
strings.ord.trappists.desc: Cistercians of the Strict Observance, reformed at La Trappe in 1664. Known for silence, manual labour and a hidden contemplative life — and, famously, for their monastery ales and cheeses.
strings.ord.carthusians.name: Carthusians
strings.ord.carthusians.desc: Founded by St Bruno in 1084 at the Grande Chartreuse, the Church's most austere order — hermits who live in solitary cells within a shared monastery. It is said they were “never reformed because never deformed.”
strings.ord.camaldolese.name: Camaldolese
strings.ord.camaldolese.desc: A Benedictine reform founded by St Romuald around 1012 at Camaldoli, blending community life with the solitude of hermits. They keep an especially contemplative, eremitical spirit.
strings.ord.norbertines.name: Norbertines (Premonstratensians)
strings.ord.norbertines.desc: Canons regular founded by St Norbert of Xanten in 1120 at Prémontré. They combine monastic prayer with active parish and pastoral ministry, following the Rule of St Augustine.
strings.sec.orders.mendicant.title: Mendicant Friars
strings.sec.orders.mendicant.summary: The preaching, begging friars who took the Gospel into the towns.
strings.art.orders.mendicant.title: Mendicant Friars
strings.art.orders.mendicant.lead: The preaching, begging friars who took the Gospel into the towns.
strings.ord.franciscans.name: Franciscans
strings.ord.franciscans.desc: Founded by St Francis of Assisi in 1209, the Order of Friars Minor embraced radical poverty and preaching. Their love of the poor, of creation and of the crib and the cross reshaped the medieval Church.
strings.ord.capuchins.name: Capuchins
strings.ord.capuchins.desc: A 16th-century reform of the Franciscans (1528) returning to strict poverty and hermit-like simplicity, marked by their long pointed hood and beard. Great preachers and missionaries among the poor.
strings.ord.conventual_franciscans.name: Conventual Franciscans
strings.ord.conventual_franciscans.desc: The branch of the Franciscan family that lives in larger urban friaries and cares for major shrines. St Maximilian Kolbe, martyr of Auschwitz, was a Conventual.
strings.ord.dominicans.name: Dominicans
strings.ord.dominicans.desc: The Order of Preachers, founded by St Dominic in 1216 to defend the faith by study and preaching. Their tradition of learning gave the Church St Thomas Aquinas and countless theologians.
strings.ord.carmelites.name: Carmelites
strings.ord.carmelites.desc: Rooted in hermits on Mount Carmel in the Holy Land, given a rule around 1209. A contemplative order under the patronage of Our Lady, devoted to prayer and the scapular.
strings.ord.discalced_carmelites.name: Discalced Carmelites
strings.ord.discalced_carmelites.desc: A reform of Carmel led by St Teresa of Ávila and St John of the Cross from 1562, restoring poverty and deep contemplative prayer. They are the great teachers of mystical prayer.
strings.ord.augustinians.name: Augustinians
strings.ord.augustinians.desc: Friars united in 1244 under the Rule of St Augustine, combining community life, study and pastoral work. Martin Luther was once one of their number.
strings.ord.servites.name: Servites (Servants of Mary)
strings.ord.servites.desc: Founded in 1233 near Florence by seven noblemen who withdrew to serve God together, the Order of Servants of Mary is devoted to Our Lady of Sorrows. Both friars and sisters carry their name.
strings.ord.trinitarians.name: Trinitarians
strings.ord.trinitarians.desc: Founded by St John of Matha in 1198 to ransom Christians captured by the Moors, giving even themselves in exchange. Their cross is red and blue.
strings.ord.mercedarians.name: Mercedarians
strings.ord.mercedarians.desc: Founded by St Peter Nolasco in 1218 in Spain, also for the redemption of captives, taking a fourth vow to give their own lives if needed.
strings.sec.orders.clerks_regular.title: Clerks Regular
strings.sec.orders.clerks_regular.summary: Priests bound by vows for reform, teaching and mission.
strings.art.orders.clerks_regular.title: Clerks Regular
strings.art.orders.clerks_regular.lead: Priests bound by vows for reform, teaching and mission.
strings.ord.jesuits.name: Jesuits
strings.ord.jesuits.desc: The Society of Jesus, founded by St Ignatius of Loyola in 1540. Marked by obedience to the pope, the Spiritual Exercises and a zeal for education and mission, they became the Church's great teachers and explorers.
strings.ord.theatines.name: Theatines
strings.ord.theatines.desc: The first of the clerks regular, founded by St Cajetan in 1524 to reform the clergy by holiness of life and pastoral care.
strings.ord.barnabites.name: Barnabites
strings.ord.barnabites.desc: Founded by St Anthony Mary Zaccaria in Milan in 1530, devoted to preaching, education and the reform of morals, taking their name from the church of St Barnabas.
strings.ord.piarists.name: Piarists
strings.ord.piarists.desc: Founded by St Joseph Calasanz in Rome in 1617, running the first free public schools for poor children. Their charism is Christian education.
strings.ord.oratorians.name: Oratorians
strings.ord.oratorians.desc: The Oratory, founded by St Philip Neri in Rome in 1575, a society of priests living together without vows, known for warmth, joy and beautiful worship.
strings.sec.orders.apostolic.title: Missionary Congregations
strings.sec.orders.apostolic.summary: The modern societies of priests and brothers for mission and charity.
strings.art.orders.apostolic.title: Missionary Congregations
strings.art.orders.apostolic.lead: The modern societies of priests and brothers for mission and charity.
strings.ord.vincentians.name: Vincentians (Lazarists)
strings.ord.vincentians.desc: The Congregation of the Mission, founded by St Vincent de Paul in 1625 to evangelise the rural poor and form good priests. Charity to the poor is their hallmark.
strings.ord.redemptorists.name: Redemptorists
strings.ord.redemptorists.desc: Founded by St Alphonsus Liguori in 1732 to preach missions to the most abandoned, especially in the countryside. Great moral theologians and preachers of God's mercy.
strings.ord.passionists.name: Passionists
strings.ord.passionists.desc: Founded by St Paul of the Cross in 1720, keeping the memory of Christ's Passion at the centre of their preaching, marked by the sign of the Passion on their habit.
strings.ord.salesians.name: Salesians of Don Bosco
strings.ord.salesians.desc: Founded by St John Bosco in Turin in 1859 for the education of poor and working-class youth. Their gentle, joyful “preventive system” has spread schools and oratories worldwide.
strings.ord.marists.name: Marists
strings.ord.marists.desc: The Society of Mary, founded in France in 1816, dedicated to missions and education under the inspiration of Our Lady. The Marist Brothers, founded by St Marcellin Champagnat, are a related teaching congregation.
strings.ord.holy_cross.name: Congregation of Holy Cross
strings.ord.holy_cross.desc: Founded by Blessed Basil Moreau in France in 1837, a congregation of priests and brothers devoted to education — best known for founding the University of Notre Dame.
strings.ord.svd.name: Divine Word Missionaries (SVD)
strings.ord.svd.desc: Founded by St Arnold Janssen in 1875, one of the largest missionary congregations, carrying the Gospel to peoples across the world.
strings.ord.omi.name: Oblates of Mary Immaculate
strings.ord.omi.desc: Founded by St Eugène de Mazenod in 1816 to preach to the poor and the far-flung, becoming great missionaries of the frozen north and beyond.
strings.ord.claretians.name: Claretians
strings.ord.claretians.desc: Founded by St Anthony Mary Claret in Spain in 1849, missionaries of the Immaculate Heart of Mary devoted to preaching and the press.
strings.ord.spiritans.name: Spiritans (Holy Ghost Fathers)
strings.ord.spiritans.desc: Founded in 1703 in Paris, a great missionary congregation especially in Africa, devoted to the Holy Spirit and the evangelisation of the poor.
strings.ord.comboni.name: Comboni Missionaries
strings.ord.comboni.desc: Founded by St Daniel Comboni in 1867 for the mission to Africa, whose motto was “Save Africa through Africa.”
strings.ord.pallottines.name: Pallottines
strings.ord.pallottines.desc: Founded by St Vincent Pallotti in Rome in 1835 to rouse all the faithful — clergy and laity alike — to apostolic zeal.
strings.ord.marians.name: Marian Fathers
strings.ord.marians.desc: Founded by St Stanislaus Papczyński in Poland in 1673, devoted to the Immaculate Conception and prayer for the dead; today great promoters of the Divine Mercy devotion.
strings.sec.orders.women.title: Congregations of Women
strings.sec.orders.women.summary: The sisters and nuns who teach, nurse and pray across the world.
strings.art.orders.women.title: Congregations of Women
strings.art.orders.women.lead: The sisters and nuns who teach, nurse and pray across the world.
strings.ord.poor_clares.name: Poor Clares
strings.ord.poor_clares.desc: Founded by St Clare of Assisi in 1212, the Franciscan Second Order — enclosed contemplative nuns living in poverty and prayer for the world.
strings.ord.carmelite_nuns.name: Discalced Carmelite Nuns
strings.ord.carmelite_nuns.desc: The contemplative nuns reformed by St Teresa of Ávila from 1562, hidden in cloistered convents and devoted wholly to prayer. St Thérèse of Lisieux is their most beloved daughter.
strings.ord.visitation.name: Visitation Sisters
strings.ord.visitation.desc: The Visitation, founded by St Francis de Sales and St Jane Frances de Chantal in 1610, gentle contemplatives to whom the Sacred Heart was revealed through St Margaret Mary.
strings.ord.ursulines.name: Ursulines
strings.ord.ursulines.desc: Founded by St Angela Merici in Brescia in 1535, the first teaching order of women, devoted to the Christian education of girls.
strings.ord.daughters_charity.name: Daughters of Charity
strings.ord.daughters_charity.desc: Founded by St Vincent de Paul and St Louise de Marillac in 1633, who took their sisters out of the cloister and into the streets to serve the poor and the sick.
strings.ord.sisters_mercy.name: Sisters of Mercy
strings.ord.sisters_mercy.desc: Founded by Venerable Catherine McAuley in Dublin in 1831 to serve the poor, the sick and the uneducated, spreading widely through the English-speaking world.
strings.ord.sisters_charity_seton.name: Sisters of Charity
strings.ord.sisters_charity_seton.desc: The first American religious community for women, founded by St Elizabeth Ann Seton in 1809, devoted to teaching and the care of the poor.
strings.ord.missionaries_charity.name: Missionaries of Charity
strings.ord.missionaries_charity.desc: Founded by St Teresa of Calcutta in 1950 to serve “the poorest of the poor.” Their white sari edged in blue is known throughout the world.
strings.ord.servite_sisters.name: Servite Sisters (Servants of Mary)
strings.ord.servite_sisters.desc: The women's branches of the Servite family, devoted like the friars to Our Lady of Sorrows, serving in nursing, teaching and the contemplative life.
strings.ord.bon_secours.name: Sisters of Bon Secours
strings.ord.bon_secours.desc: Founded in Paris in 1824 to nurse the sick in their own homes — “bon secours” meaning good, helping care. They remain devoted to healthcare and compassion.
strings.ord.salesian_sisters.name: Salesian Sisters
strings.ord.salesian_sisters.desc: The Daughters of Mary Help of Christians, founded by St John Bosco and St Mary Mazzarello in 1872, bringing Don Bosco's joyful education to girls.
strings.ord.little_sisters_poor.name: Little Sisters of the Poor
strings.ord.little_sisters_poor.desc: Founded by St Jeanne Jugan in France in 1839 to care for the elderly poor, begging door to door to support the aged in their homes.
strings.ord.good_shepherd.name: Good Shepherd Sisters
strings.ord.good_shepherd.desc: Founded by St Mary Euphrasia Pelletier in 1835, devoted to women and girls in difficulty, seeking out the one lost sheep.
strings.ord.presentation.name: Presentation Sisters
strings.ord.presentation.desc: Founded by Venerable Nano Nagle in Cork in 1775 to teach the poor children of Ireland in defiance of the penal laws.
strings.ord.loreto_ibvm.name: Loreto Sisters (IBVM)
strings.ord.loreto_ibvm.desc: The Institute of the Blessed Virgin Mary, founded by Venerable Mary Ward in 1609, a pioneering unenclosed order of women teachers.
strings.ord.ssnd.name: School Sisters of Notre Dame
strings.ord.ssnd.desc: Founded in Bavaria in 1833 by Blessed Theresa Gerhardinger, teaching sisters devoted to the education of girls and the poor.
strings.ord.sisters_st_joseph.name: Sisters of St Joseph
strings.ord.sisters_st_joseph.desc: Founded at Le Puy in France in 1650, one of the most widespread congregations, serving “the dear neighbour” in every kind of need.
